Ferhat Ay: The Ay lab uses computational and statistical modeling to study how genes are turned on and off, and how this goes wrong in diseases like infections and immune disorders. A major focus is the 3D shape of the genome — how DNA folds inside the nucleus — using data from high-throughput chromatin conformation techniques like Hi-C and HiChIP to see how that folding affects development and disease. The lab builds new computational tools, drawing on statistics, graph theory, data mining, and machine learning, to analyze these large genomic datasets. They also work on mapping regulatory networks, predicting which DNA switches (enhancers) control which genes, forecasting gene activity levels, and analyzing single-cell data. This matters because understanding how genes are regulated at this structural level could reveal new ways to diagnose and treat disease.
Christopher Benedict: The Benedict lab studies cytomegalovirus (CMV), a common herpesvirus that infects over half of people without making most of them sick, and how it interacts with the immune system. They discovered a new viral protein complex called GATE that helps CMV enter cells and suppress immune defenses, a discovery relevant to future vaccine development. The lab also studies TRAIL, an immune signaling molecule, and its surprising connection to CMV, as well as how CMV can hijack immune checkpoint proteins. Notably, CMV infection causes the body to dedicate an unusually large fraction of its T cells to fighting it — more than any other known virus — and the lab has shown these T cells can be redirected to attack pancreatic cancer instead, suggesting CMV immunity could be repurposed as an off-the-shelf cancer therapy.
Hilde Cheroutre: The Cheroutre lab studies how the immune system protects the body's interfaces with the outside world, such as the skin, lungs, mouth, and especially the intestine, where a huge surface is constantly exposed to food and bacteria. A central question is how the immune system tells the difference between harmless food and bacteria versus dangerous pathogens, and what goes wrong when it fails, since that failure can cause disease. The lab focuses heavily on specialized T cells living in the gut lining and studies conditions like celiac disease, where immune cells wrongly attack gluten. They also study immune memory cells that form after fighting off tumors or infections and can react quickly if the same threat returns, which is relevant to preventing cancer recurrence.
Shane Crotty: The Crotty lab studies how the immune system responds to vaccines, aiming to design better ones for diseases including HIV, influenza, strep throat, and COVID-19. A key discovery was that spacing out vaccine doses over time, rather than giving them all at once, produces stronger antibody responses because it lets immune cells repeatedly refine their targeting in structures called germinal centers. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the lab performed some of the first detailed studies of how the immune system responds to SARS-CoV-2, showing that T cells and antibodies together recognize many different parts of the virus, including the spike protein used in most vaccines. They also found that many unexposed people had some pre-existing immune memory from prior common-cold coronavirus infections, which may explain differences in COVID-19 severity between individuals.
Einav: The Einav lab tackles a long-standing puzzle in vaccine research: why the same vaccine produces a strong immune response in some people but almost none in others. Rather than studying single pieces of the immune system in isolation, the lab builds computational, systems-level models using machine learning and biophysics to analyze large amounts of existing immunology data. Their goal is a form of personalized medicine that uses a person's own antibody profile to predict which vaccine or strain would protect them best, and to understand tradeoffs such as whether a stronger immune response is also a longer-lasting one. Ultimately, they aim to uncover general, predictive 'laws' governing how the immune system responds to vaccination, which could guide the design of more effective and personalized vaccines.
Alba Grifoni: The Grifoni lab studies how T cells, a key part of the immune system, respond to viral infections and vaccines, with a focus on coronaviruses. As part of LJI's Coronavirus Taskforce, the lab has mapped which parts of SARS-CoV-2 are recognized by T cells and shown that T cell immunity from vaccination remains effective against variants like Omicron, informing future vaccine design. They are now investigating what a vaccine effective against many different coronaviruses at once would need to target. The lab has also applied this fast-response approach to emerging outbreaks, showing that an existing smallpox vaccine could also train T cells to recognize mpox, and more broadly studies how the immune system can be harnessed to fight families of viruses such as Lassa fever and hantavirus, supporting pandemic preparedness.
Hastie: The Hastie lab uses structural biology to study the shape and function of proteins on the surface of viruses, particularly how they interact with antibodies from the immune system. By determining these structures in molecular detail, the lab aims to understand how the human immune system naturally fights viral infection and to expose weaknesses in viral proteins that are normally well-hidden. This structural knowledge feeds into a high-throughput platform developed in the lab to rapidly identify promising antibodies for use as therapies or diagnostics, sometimes within weeks of a new virus emerging. One applied focus has been developing an antibody-based treatment against New World Arenaviruses, a family of dangerous rodent-borne viruses for which no vaccines or treatments currently exist.
Patrick Hogan: The Hogan lab studies how proteins interact with each other and with DNA inside cells to switch genes on, at a nano-scale level of detail, focusing especially on T cells, the immune system's infection-fighting white blood cells. A major theme is how calcium entering a T cell triggers the gene activity needed to fight infections and cancer. The lab made a landmark discovery of the protein ORAI1, which forms the channel that lets calcium into T cells, after finding it was mutated in children with severe immune deficiency. This work suggests that drugs targeting this calcium channel could one day help treat transplant rejection and autoimmune diseases, and the lab has also explored how to prevent cancer-fighting T cells from losing effectiveness over time.
Mitchell Kronenberg: The Kronenberg lab studies mucosal immunity, focusing on how the immune system protects and regulates the lining of the gut and other vulnerable organs. A major research area involves Vα14 invariant NKT cells, an unusual population of T lymphocytes with distinctive properties, as well as broader questions in inflammatory bowel disease. In collaboration with other LJI labs, they investigate how immune cells behave abnormally in autoimmune conditions such as ulcerative colitis and diseases affecting the bile ducts, and how immune cells can be tuned by diet-related factors like sugar and fat. The lab's goal is to understand how the gut immune system normally protects the body and how its breakdown contributes to inflammatory and autoimmune disease.
Li: The Li lab uses structural immunology to visualize, at high resolution, how viruses and the immune system interact at the molecular level, aiming to turn these insights into new vaccines and therapies. Their research spans how viruses like arenaviruses hijack receptors on human cells to cause infection, how antibodies and T-cell receptors recognize infected or cancerous cells, and how immune signaling molecules can be tuned to fight inflammation. Concrete projects include designing new immunogens (vaccine components) for Lassa virus and combining rare neutralizing antibodies into cocktail therapies, building on prior work resolving detailed structures of viral proteins bound to antibodies for viruses including SARS-CoV-2 and LCMV. The broader goal is to translate these molecular blueprints into treatments for infections, autoimmune disease, and cancer.
Samuel Myers: The Myers lab studies how proteins inside immune cells are chemically modified after they're made (called post-translational modifications, or PTMs), and how these modifications work together to control cell behavior. Using protein mass spectrometry and quantitative proteomics, combined with genomics and chemical biology, the lab traces how these signals flow through cells to control gene expression, ultimately determining whether an immune cell attacks a threat or tolerates harmless microbes and the body's own tissues. Because only a small number of these modifications have been well studied, the lab aims to uncover many more that have gone unnoticed. This matters because understanding these signaling networks could improve treatment of autoimmune disorders as well as cardiovascular disease, neurodegeneration, and cancer.
Bjoern Peters: The Peters lab develops computational tools to answer fundamental questions in immunology, with a major focus on identifying which specific molecular targets (epitopes) the immune system recognizes during infection, vaccination, or disease. One research area compares immune cells from healthy versus diseased individuals at the single-cell level, using transcriptomic, proteomic, and genomic data, often isolating cells based on disease-specific epitopes identified by algorithms built in the lab. This work spans conditions such as tuberculosis, whooping cough, food allergies, and cancer, and has shown that essentially all cancer patients mount some immune response to their tumors, a finding relevant to expanding personalized immunotherapy. The lab also helps maintain the Immune Epitope Database, a major public resource supporting immunology research worldwide.
